organizations.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

recommendations.title: Influenza (Flu) Vaccine — Annual
recommendations.recommendation_text: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months of age and older who does not have contraindications. Adults 65 years and older should preferentially receive a higher-dose or adjuvanted influenza vaccine (high-dose inactivated, recombinant, or adjuvanted inactivated).
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu shot every year, ideally by the end of October. Adults 65 and older should get one of the stronger flu vaccines made for older adults (high-dose or adjuvanted) — ask your pharmacist or doctor.

recommendations.title: COVID-19 Vaccine — Updated Annual Dose
recommendations.recommendation_text: Everyone 6 months of age and older should receive an updated (current-season) COVID-19 vaccine. Older adults and immunocompromised persons may be eligible for additional doses during the season.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Everyone 6 months and older should get the updated COVID-19 vaccine each year, usually in the fall. If you are 65 or older or have a weakened immune system, ask your doctor whether an extra dose during the season makes sense for you.

recommendations.title: Tdap / Td (Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Adults who have never received Tdap should receive one dose of Tdap, followed by a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years. Pregnant persons should receive one dose of Tdap during every pregnancy, optimally between 27 and 36 weeks of gestation, regardless of prior Tdap history.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults need a tetanus-diphtheria booster every 10 years; at least one of those should be a Tdap (which also covers whooping cough). If you are pregnant, you should get a Tdap during each pregnancy between weeks 27 and 36 — this passes whooping cough protection to your newborn.

recommendations.title: Shingles Vaccine (Recombinant Zoster Vaccine, Shingrix)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix) are recommended for adults 50 years and older, given 2 to 6 months apart. Adults 19 years and older who are immunocompromised should also receive the 2-dose series.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 50 and older should get the Shingrix shingles vaccine — 2 shots, 2 to 6 months apart. It is recommended even if you already had shingles or the older shingles vaccine. Shingles can cause long-lasting nerve pain; Shingrix is more than 90% effective at preventing it.

recommendations.title: Pneumococcal Vaccine (PCV15, PCV20, or PCV21)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccination is recommended for all adults 50 years and older who have not previously received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (single dose of PCV20 or PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23). Adults 19–49 with certain chronic or immunocompromising conditions should also be vaccinated. Guidance was lowered from age 65 to age 50 by ACIP in October 2024.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 50 and older should get a pneumococcal (pneumonia) vaccine if they have not had one — usually a single shot. Younger adults with conditions like diabetes, heart or lung disease, or a weakened immune system should get it earlier. Ask your doctor which product and schedule applies to you.

recommendations.title: HPV Vaccine (Gardasil 9)
recommendations.recommendation_text: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended at age 11–12 years, with catch-up vaccination recommended for all persons through age 26 years who were not adequately vaccinated. For adults aged 27 through 45 years, vaccination is based on shared clinical decision-making with a clinician.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: The HPV vaccine prevents most cervical and several other cancers. It is routinely given at ages 11–12, and catch-up vaccination is recommended for everyone through age 26 who missed it. Adults 27–45 can discuss with their doctor whether the vaccine would still benefit them.

recommendations.title: Hepatitis A Vaccine
recommendations.recommendation_text: Hepatitis A vaccination (2-dose series, 6–12 months apart) is recommended for adults at increased risk, including travelers to endemic countries, men who have sex with men, persons who use injection or non-injection drugs, persons experiencing homelessness, persons with chronic liver disease, and anyone who requests protection.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: The hepatitis A vaccine (2 shots, 6 months apart) is recommended for adults at higher risk — including travelers to certain countries, people with chronic liver disease, people who use drugs, and people experiencing homelessness. Any adult who wants protection can get it.

recommendations.title: Hepatitis B Vaccine
recommendations.recommendation_text: Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all adults aged 19 through 59 years. Adults 60 years and older with risk factors (diabetes, chronic liver disease, HIV, sexual or household exposure risk, healthcare or public safety work, travel to endemic areas, incarceration, homelessness) should be vaccinated; adults 60+ without risk factors may be vaccinated.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: All adults 19–59 should be vaccinated against hepatitis B (usually 2 or 3 shots depending on the product). Adults 60 and older with risk factors — such as diabetes, liver disease, or possible exposure through work, travel, or household contact — should also get it. Hepatitis B can silently damage the liver for years.

recommendations.title: Meningococcal ACWY Vaccine (MenACWY)
recommendations.recommendation_text: MenACWY vaccination is recommended for adults with certain risk conditions, including asplenia or complement deficiency, complement inhibitor use, HIV infection, microbiologists with routine Neisseria meningitidis exposure, travelers to hyperendemic or epidemic areas, and first-year college students living in residence halls who were not vaccinated at age 16 or older.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: The meningococcal ACWY vaccine protects against a rare but life-threatening bacterial infection. It is recommended for people without a working spleen, those with certain immune conditions or HIV, lab workers exposed to the bacteria, travelers to parts of Africa, and college freshmen living in dorms who were not vaccinated at 16 or older.

recommendations.title: Meningococcal B Vaccine (MenB)
recommendations.recommendation_text: MenB vaccination is recommended for persons 10 years and older with asplenia, complement deficiency, complement inhibitor use, or during a serogroup B outbreak. For adolescents and young adults aged 16–23 years (preferred age 16–18), MenB vaccination is based on shared clinical decision-making.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: The meningococcal B vaccine is recommended for people with certain immune or spleen conditions and during outbreaks. Young people aged 16–23 (ideally 16–18) can decide together with their doctor whether to get it — worth discussing especially before living in college dorms.

recommendations.title: RSV Vaccine (Respiratory Syncytial Virus)
recommendations.recommendation_text: A single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for all adults 75 years and older, and for adults 60–74 years at increased risk for severe RSV disease (chronic heart or lung disease, immunocompromise, nursing home residence). This reflects the June 2024 ACIP update, which replaced the 2023 shared clinical decision-making approach for adults 60+.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: A one-time RSV vaccine is recommended for everyone 75 and older, and for adults 60–74 with conditions like chronic heart or lung disease, a weakened immune system, or who live in a nursing home. RSV can cause serious lung illness in older adults.
